name: Lerwick
title: Lerwick Ship Thickness Gauging | Fishing, Ferry & Offshore
description: Ultrasonic thickness measurement in Lerwick for pelagic trawlers, ferries, offshore vessels and barges: hull plating, fish holds, tanks, decks and piping.
h1: Hull and Tank Thickness Measurement for Ships Calling at Lerwick
intro: Lerwick is Shetland's main harbour and its busiest working waterfront: pelagic and whitefish boats land at the fish market, the overnight ferry from Aberdeen berths at Holmsgarth, supply vessels work from Greenhead, and decommissioned topsides come ashore at Dales Voe. Each fleet has quiet days alongside, between fishing trips, refits or project mobilisations, and those days are when hull, tank and piping gauging gets done. Our technicians are flown out from India for the job and join the vessel at her berth.

highlights.p: Shetland's pelagic trawlers and whitefish boats spend most of the year at sea and come alongside in Lerwick to land their catch and refit. Refrigerated sea-water tanks, fish holds, shell and deck plating can be gauged in the days a boat is tied up between trips.

Supply vessels, standby vessels and the transport barges and heavy-lift ships that bring topsides to Dales Voe and Greenhead often lie alongside for days during mobilisation or after an offload. That time suits deck, tank and crane-foundation checks with UT and magnetic particle testing.

highlights.h: Deep, sheltered water in Bressay Sound
highlights.p: With the island of Bressay sheltering the harbour and outer harbour areas deeper than fifty metres, Lerwick can hold large ships at anchor or on its berths in most weather, which gives a team on board a workable platform when the open sea outside is rough.

port.h: Lerwick: Shetland's harbour for fish, ferries and the offshore industry
p: Lerwick faces east across Bressay Sound, the strait between Mainland Shetland and the island of Bressay, and the harbour can be entered from both the north and the south ends of the sound. Bressay shelters it from easterly seas while Mainland breaks the Atlantic westerlies, and the harbour has two outer areas with very deep water where ships can anchor, deballast or prepare heavy lifts. Lerwick Port Authority runs every quay as a common-user berth, and the harbour works around the clock in all seasons. Shetland winters bring long nights and strong gales rather than ice, so the planning constraint is weather and daylight on deck, not freezing water. Ships waiting for a berth, or for better conditions offshore, often anchor in the sound until the weather or their schedule allows them to move.

The fishing industry gives Lerwick much of its character. Shetland is one of Britain's leading seafood centres, and the harbour handles landings, the fish market's electronic auction, processing and onward shipment. The pelagic fleet, large refrigerated trawlers working mackerel and herring, sits alongside between seasons, while whitefish boats land through the year. NorthLink's overnight ro-pax ferries link Lerwick with Kirkwall and Aberdeen, and freight ships bring fuel, feed and general cargo to the islands. Offshore supply and standby vessels serving fields east and west of Shetland use the Greenhead base. Around a hundred cruise ships call in a typical season, berthing at the quays or anchoring in the sound, and the harbour's own tugs and pilot boats keep all of this moving.

Decommissioning is the newer trade. Lerwick was among the first UK ports to take significant volumes of redundant offshore structures, and its two licensed quayside sites at Dales Voe and Greenhead have received topsides and module frames lifted from North Sea fields, the largest so far being the Ninian Northern topside landed at Dales Voe in 2020. Heavy-transport ships, cargo barges and the tugs that tow them spend days alongside while loads are moved ashore, and a planned ultra-deep water quay at Dales Voe is intended to let semi-submersible crane vessels offload directly. For inspection this mix means very different vessels in the same week: a trawler in for a refit, a ferry between sailings, a barge after a heavy offload, and a supply ship waiting for her next charter.

facilities.h: Where vessels are gauged in and around Lerwick harbour
p: Lerwick has no drydock for seagoing ships, so most gauging here happens afloat. Fishing boats are the exception: the slipway in the harbour and the engineering firms that maintain the fleet can haul smaller craft out of the water, and a hull on the slip is the best chance to gauge bottom shell and sea chests from outside. Larger pelagic trawlers, ferries and offshore vessels go to yards on the Scottish mainland, in Norway or in Denmark for their dockings, and a Lerwick call shortly before that docking is the natural moment to take the readings that become the yard's steel list.

Ferries are gauged during the hours they lie alongside at Holmsgarth between sailings, which suits deck, car-deck, void-space and piping work planned in short blocks. Supply vessels and project ships at Greenhead and Dales Voe lie on open quays with room to stage equipment, and the time they spend waiting on weather or loading suits a full scope on cargo tanks and working decks. The deep outer anchorages give a further option for ships that do not need a berth, with the agent arranging boat transfers. Whichever berth is used, gas-freeing and permits for tank entry are arranged by the ship before the team boards.
list: Holmsgarth ferry terminal — deck, void-space and piping gauging on ro-pax ferries during their time alongside between sailings.
Fish market and fishing quays — fish hold, refrigerated sea-water tank and shell gauging on trawlers tied up between trips.
The harbour slipway — bottom shell, keel and sea-chest readings on smaller fishing boats and workboats hauled out for repair.
Greenhead base — cargo tank, working-deck and crane-foundation checks on supply and standby vessels between charters.
Dales Voe quay — deck and structure gauging plus crack detection on transport barges and heavy-lift ships after offloading.
Bressay Sound and the outer harbour anchorages — targeted gauging by boat transfer on ships waiting for a berth or for weather.

context.h: Port state control, fisheries and the North Atlantic setting
p: Inspections of foreign-flagged ships at Lerwick are made by the Maritime and Coastguard Agency, which applies Paris MoU targeting under UK law. Many of the vessels that matter most here sit largely outside that regime, though: fishing vessels are covered by the UK's own fishing vessel safety rules, ferries by passenger-ship surveys, and offshore vessels by charterer audits as well as class. For a superintendent, that means the reason for gauging varies by fleet. A trawler owner may want hull and fish-hold readings before an insurance survey or a sale, a ferry operator before the annual passenger-ship inspection, and a supply-vessel owner before a charterer's audit.

Weather is the other regulator. Lerwick lies at around sixty degrees north, open to North Atlantic and North Sea storms, and winter gales can keep ships in port for days or stop boat transfers at the anchorage altogether. Daylight shrinks to under six hours in midwinter, which matters for deck and shell work but not for tank interiors under lighting. Summer is the busiest season for cruise calls and many offshore campaigns, while the pelagic fleet's quiet months follow the mackerel and herring seasons. Planning a Lerwick job around those patterns, with a fallback day built in, avoids a team arriving to find the vessel gone or the anchorage closed.

jobs.h: Gauging jobs that come up in Lerwick
jobs.p: Work in Lerwick tends to follow the fleets rather than a survey calendar. A fishing company wants to know the condition of a trawler's holds before committing to a refit; a project manager needs a barge's deck checked after a heavy load has gone ashore; a ferry operator plans piping renewals for a winter docking on the mainland. We agree the scope and the order of work with the master or the owner's representative beforehand, so that the readings that decide the next repair are taken first and the rest fills the remaining time alongside. Tanks and holds are cleaned and certified for entry before we arrive.
list: Fish hold and refrigerated sea-water tank gauging on a pelagic trawler tied up between the mackerel and herring seasons, ahead of a yard visit abroad.
Pre-purchase hull gauging on a second-hand whitefish boat being bought into the Shetland fleet.
Car-deck, void-space and sea-water piping UT on a ro-pax ferry during her lay-over at Holmsgarth.
Deck plating and sea-fastening point crack detection on a transport barge after a topside offload at Dales Voe.
Cargo tank and working-deck survey on a standby or supply vessel waiting at Greenhead for her next charter.

logistics: The usual route for the team is a flight to Aberdeen, Edinburgh or Glasgow and an onward Loganair connection to Sumburgh, Shetland's main airport at the southern tip of Mainland, followed by the drive north to Lerwick. NorthLink's overnight ferry from Aberdeen is the alternative when flights are disrupted by weather or when heavier equipment travels with the team. Technicians mobilise from India on UK visas, so a booking made well ahead of the vessel's expected days in port helps. Quay access and harbour boat transfers are organised through the ship's agent and Lerwick Port Authority.

faqs.q: Can a fishing vessel's refrigerated sea-water tanks be gauged in Lerwick?
faqs.a: Yes, once the tanks are pumped out, washed and ventilated. RSW tanks see cold, wet service and their coatings can hide pitting until it is well advanced, so readings are taken wherever the steel can be reached and compared with earlier surveys. We plan the work with the skipper for the days between trips, and record readings on the tank plans so a yard can plan repairs before the boat sails south.

faqs.q: Can a ship be drydocked in Lerwick for a renewal survey?
faqs.a: Not a seagoing ship. Smaller fishing boats and workboats can be hauled out on the slipway in Lerwick, but ferries, pelagic trawlers and offshore vessels dock on the Scottish mainland or in Norway or Denmark. A Lerwick call before that docking is a good moment for pre-docking gauging, because the steel estimate then reaches the yard before the ship does and renewal can be planned rather than discovered.

faqs.q: Can you work on a ship anchored in Bressay Sound?
faqs.a: Yes, with boat transfers arranged by the agent and the port authority, when the weather allows a safe boarding. The sound is well sheltered, but strong winds from some directions can still stop transfers, so the scope is ordered with the most important readings first. Anchorage work suits deck plating, air pipes and tanks the crew has prepared; full tank programmes are better done alongside.

faqs.q: Do you inspect barges and transport vessels used for decommissioning at Dales Voe?
faqs.a: Yes. After a heavy offload, owners and charterers often want deck plating, sea-fastening points and the structure beneath the load area checked before the next job. We combine thickness readings with magnetic particle testing on welds at grillage and sea-fastening attachments, and report against the vessel's frame and deck plan, so damage from the load can be separated from older wastage.

faqs.q: What happens if weather stops the team reaching Shetland?
faqs.a: Flights to Sumburgh and the overnight ferry are both affected by severe weather, particularly in winter, so we plan a spare day into the schedule and keep in touch with the agent about the vessel's movements. If the ship's time in port shortens, the scope agreed in advance tells us which readings to take first, and any remaining work can move to the vessel's next port call.
